area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a skidding, cross-controlled turn steepens its own bank and can roll the airplane over at the stall, demonstrate the stall from the right seat at a safe altitude with power off, recover before a spin develops, and teach a learner to spot and avoid the base-to-final setup that causes it.
why: The skidding cross-control stall is most likely in a poorly flown base-to-final turn, comes with very little warning and can be deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. It is a demonstration-only maneuver that only flight instructor applicants may be asked to perform on a practical test, but every pilot should know how it happens, how to recognize it and how to recover [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. You will be the one who shows it to your learners, so your demonstration is their only safe look at it.

prereading.what: The cross-control stall: objective, the base-to-final setup, the entry and recovery, and the 18 common stall errors.
prereading.label: AFH 5-20 to 5-21

prereading.what: Spin awareness, spin phases, the spin recovery template and spin approval placards.
prereading.label: AFH 5-22 to 5-25

prereading.what: How a slip and a skid feel and look, and why the outside wing is faster in a turn (overbanking tendency).
prereading.label: AFH 3-13 to 3-14

prereading.what: Gliding turns: lighter rudder forces, overcontrol, and the two cross-control hazards near the ground.
prereading.label: AFH 3-23 to 3-24

prereading.what: Forces in turns: normal, slipping and skidding turns (Figure 5-35).
prereading.label: PHAK 5-23 to 5-24

prereading.what: Types of stalls, recovery, spins, the primary cause of inadvertent spins and spin recovery.
prereading.label: AC 61-67C 104 to 111

prereading.what: Learner practice, positive exchange of flight controls, guarding the controls and why distractions cause stall/spin accidents.
prereading.label: AIH 9-8 to 9-10

warmup: Think first: your learner flies a left pattern with a strong wind pushing them toward the runway on base. They turn final late, see the nose pointing past the centerline, and you feel their left foot push hard while the yoke goes right and back. Nothing has happened yet. What is about to happen to the left wing, and why? What will you say right now, and what will you change in your next ground lesson so they never do it solo?

key_terms.def: A stall where the critical AOA is exceeded with aileron pressure one way and rudder pressure the other way, so the airplane is uncoordinated [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Aileron deflection in the opposite direction of rudder deflection [[24:377|AFH Glossary]].
A turn where centrifugal force is greater than the horizontal lift component; the rate of turn is too great for the bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
A turn where the airplane is banked too much for its rate of turn, so the horizontal lift component is greater than centrifugal force [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].
Rudder pressure applied toward the direction of the turn, the input that turns a base-to-final overshoot into a skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
The outside wing travels faster than the inside wing, makes more lift and tends to steepen the bank [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
A turn with a bank between about 20 and 45 degrees, where the airplane tends to hold its bank with neutral ailerons [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
An aggravated stall that can follow a stall, with the airplane in a downward corkscrew path; at least one wing is stalled [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
The part of a spin from the stall and the start of rotation until the spin is fully developed [[13:12|AC 61-67C 110a]].
A maneuver the instructor shows for awareness; for the cross-control stall, only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform it on a practical test [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
The safest action for an overshoot of the base-to-final turn, instead of steepening or skidding the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The objective of the cross-control stall demonstration is to show what uncoordinated flight does to stall behavior, and why turns must stay coordinated [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Your learner does not need to master it as a checkride maneuver. They need to know the setup that leads to it, how to recognize it, how to avoid it and how to recover [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

The CFI ACS says the flight instructor normally demonstrates Tasks F, G and H (cross-control, elevator trim and secondary stalls) to learners for familiarization and stall/spin awareness, and that private and commercial certification does not include them (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X note). AC 61-67C's training plan goes further: do stalls in gliding turns that simulate base to final, from a coordinated turn, a slipping turn and a skidding turn, and explain the ball position and the airplane's behavior in each [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200d]].

This lesson assumes you have the general stall material from the Power-Off Stalls lesson (AI.X.C): critical AOA, load factor, stall cues and the recovery template. Here we only add what is special about this stall: the crossed controls, why the low wing goes first, how to set it up safely and how to stop it before a spin.

callout.text: On the checkride, describing and demonstrating the conditions that lead to a cross-controlled stall, for future avoidance, is its own skill element (AI.X.F.S8). Plan the words, not just the control inputs.

Application: open the ground brief with the pattern, not the maneuver. Draw a base leg with a tailwind, show the overshoot, and ask the learner what they would do. Then show how the demonstration copies that turn at a safe altitude.

check.q: Is the cross-control stall part of the private or commercial practical test?
check.a: No. The CFI ACS says private and commercial certification does not include it (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X note), and only flight instructor applicants may be required to perform it [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Start the aerodynamics with a plain turn. Banking tilts the lift, and its horizontal part turns the airplane; the rudder only lines the nose and tail up with the relative wind [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]] [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]. In a correct turn the horizontal lift equals centrifugal force [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

head: Turn
What is out of balance
How to fix it
rows: Coordinated
Horizontal lift equals centrifugal force
Nothing; ball centered [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]
Slipping
Too much bank for the rate of turn; horizontal lift is greater than centrifugal force
Less bank, more rate of turn, or both [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]
Skidding
Rate of turn too great for the bank; centrifugal force is greater than horizontal lift
Less rate of turn, more bank, or both [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]]

body.p: Cross controlled means the aileron is deflected one way and the rudder the other [[24:377|AFH Glossary]]. In the dangerous base-to-final version the pilot holds inside rudder to swing the nose and opposite aileron to stop the bank from steepening: a skid with crossed controls [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Why the bank wants to steepen. In a turn the outside wing travels a longer path in the same time, so it is faster and makes more lift; the difference grows as the turn gets tighter. This overbanking tendency is held with opposite aileron [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. When rudder yaws the airplane, the wing that swings forward gains airspeed [[1:117|PHAK 5-20]]. The AFH puts it directly for a glide: excessive rudder leads to increased lift on the outside wing and banks the airplane in the direction of the rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. In the base-to-final skid the lift difference between the inside and outside wing grows and the bank increases on its own [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Power-off glides make this worse. In a gliding turn there is no propeller slipstream and the rudder forces are lighter, so a learner used to powered flight may push too much rudder, causing slips and skids [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The AFH lists 'skidding or slipping during gliding turns and not recognizing the difference in rudder forces with and without power' as a common error [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

callout.text: Skid = rate too great for the bank, nose yawed into the turn, ball to the outside. Slip = bank too great for the rate, ball to the inside.

check.q: In a skidding turn, which is larger: the horizontal component of lift or centrifugal force?
check.a: Centrifugal force; the rate of turn is too great for the angle of bank [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

chunks.title: Why the bank steepens and the airplane rolls over

body.p: Walk the learner through the AFH chain of events, one control at a time [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]:

bullets: 1. Overshoot: a tailwind on base gives a higher groundspeed, so the pilot turns late or too shallow and overshoots the centerline.
2. Inside rudder: to bring the nose around without more bank, the pilot pushes rudder toward the turn.
3. Bank grows: the lift difference between the inside and outside wing grows, and the bank steepens on its own.
4. Opposite aileron: the pilot holds the bank with aileron away from the turn. Controls are now crossed.
5. Nose drops: the nose slices down through the horizon.
6. Pull: the natural reaction is back elevator, which raises the AOA toward critical.
7. Stall: with these inputs, the airplane may rapidly enter a spin.

body.p: What the learner sees at the stall: the nose may pitch down, the bank may change suddenly, and the airplane may keep rolling to an inverted attitude, which is usually the beginning of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. It can happen with very little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Why the roll goes toward the low wing. What the sources state directly: inside rudder yaws the outside wing forward and gives it more lift [[1:117|PHAK 5-20]], the excess rudder banks the airplane toward the rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]], in a skid the bank may increase further to a potentially dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]], and at the stall the airplane may keep rolling toward inverted [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. None of the AFH, PHAK or AC 61-67C says in words which wing stalls first in a skid. Application, offered as a reasoned picture and not tested in the quiz: the inside wing is the slower wing [[24:75|AFH 3-14]], and the opposite aileron that holds the bank puts its aileron down, which the AFH says gives a wing a greater AOA and a more complete stall at the tip [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. So the low wing is the likely one to reach the critical AOA first.

From stall to spin. A spin needs a stall plus sideslip or yaw at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can enter a spin rotating in the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. AC 61-67C says the same: the spin from cross controlling usually rotates the way the rudder is applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. In a spin the descending wing is more stalled than the rising one [[13:11|AC 61-67C 107]].

Compare the slip. In a slipping turning stall, the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly; in a skid the bank may increase further to a dangerous attitude [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. That difference is why the skid near the ground is the killer: the roll goes toward the ground and toward the turn the pilot was already in.

callout.text: The pilot who caused the yaw with the rudder may not realize the critical AOA has been exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: A skidding left turn stalls with right aileron held. Which way will a resulting spin usually rotate, and why?
check.a: Left, the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

body.p: Flight situations where an unintentional cross-controlled stall may occur (K2). Teach each as a story the learner will recognize in their own pattern:

head: Situation
How the cross-control develops
What to teach instead
rows: Base-to-final overshoot
Tailwind on base, late or shallow turn, then steeper bank, more back pressure and inside rudder to line up [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Go around; below 30 degrees of bank at that low altitude; never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Rushing the turn for traffic
A pilot trying to gain distance from another aircraft may make an overly steep turn to final [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
If rushing the turn, abandon the approach and go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]]
Avoiding a steep bank in the pattern
The pilot rudders the airplane around (skids) so as not to overshoot or use much bank [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]
Plan the pattern for the wind: the AFH asks pilots to consider tailwinds on downwind so the base leg works out [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Low gliding steep turn after an engine failure
Rudder toward the bank while pulling to hold altitude can quickly become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Hold glide speed; accept the descent; coordinated, shallow turns
Power-off landing approach
Too much rudder banks the airplane, opposite aileron holds the bank, back pressure added: a fully developed cross-control condition [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Light, coordinated rudder in glides; watch the ball
Stretching a power-off approach
Skidding turns in an effort to increase gliding distance [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Turn with coordinated controls and choose a closer spot

body.p: This is not rare. Many stall/spin accidents have happened in power-off situations such as crossed control turns from base leg to final [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. More than 25 percent of general aviation fatal accidents happen in the maneuvering phase, and half of those involve stall/spin [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

callout.text: A stall in the power-off approach cross-control situation almost certainly results in a rapid and unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. The demonstration exists so your learner sees the start of it with 3,000 ft under them, never in the pattern.

Application: when your learner overshoots final on a real approach, make the go-around call yourself the first few times, then have them make it. That is S8 in action: 'conditions that lead to a cross-controlled stall, for future avoidance'.

check.q: What does the AFH call the safest action for an overshoot of the base-to-final turn?

body.p: Recognition of cross-controlled stalls (K3) is harder than for a coordinated stall, because this stall can come with very little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Teach the learner the cues that come before it, so they never get to the stall itself:

bullets: Feel: in a skid the pilot is pushed toward the outside of the turn [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Ball: in a skid the ball goes to the outside of the turn [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
Controls: rudder pushed toward the turn while aileron is held away from it, plus growing back pressure [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Picture: the bank wants to steepen and the nose slices down through the horizon [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Instruments: in uncoordinated flight the pitot-static instruments, especially the altimeter and airspeed indicator, are unreliable, so the pilot may not know the critical AOA is near until the stall warning sounds [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].
Stall: buffet or the stall horn if the airplane has time to give them, then a sudden change in bank and nose drop [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Acknowledge the cues (S6). During your demonstration say each cue aloud the moment it appears: 'ball outside, skidding', 'horn', 'buffet', 'wing dropping'. Your voice gives the learner a sequence to remember, and lets the evaluator see you recognized it.

callout.text: Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]. If a spin starts, the ball is no help at all: its movement depends on where it is mounted, not on the spin direction; use the turn indicator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

check.q: Your learner says, 'I'll watch the airspeed, so I'll know when it is about to stall.' Why is that weak in a skid?
check.a: In uncoordinated flight the airspeed indicator and altimeter are unreliable, so the stall may come before the pilot expects it [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

chunks.title: Entry procedure and minimum entry altitude

body.p: Entry procedure (K4), from the AFH [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], matched to the ACS skill elements:

head: Step
What you do
Source
rows: Altitude
Pick an entry altitude safe for entry and recovery in the event of a spin; the ACS requires the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet AGL (S2)
Clear
Clear the area of other traffic while slowly retarding the throttle (S1)
Configure
Gear down if retractable, close the throttle (S3). Do not extend flaps, to avoid exceeding the airplane's limitations
Glide
Hold altitude until the airspeed approaches normal glide speed, then glide and retrim (S4)
Turn
Once stable, roll into a medium-banked turn, simulating a final approach turn that overshoots the centerline (S5)
Cross the controls
Smoothly add excessive rudder toward the turn, hold the bank constant with opposite aileron, and add back elevator to keep the nose from lowering (S5)
Hold to the stall
Keep increasing all these pressures until the airplane stalls, or recover at the first indication if that is what the evaluator asked for (S7)

body.p: Minimum entry altitude. The ACS number for this Task is higher than the handbook numbers. The AFH recommends practicing stalls at an altitude that allows recovery no lower than 1,500 feet AGL for single-engine airplanes [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and starting spins high enough to complete recovery at or above 1,500 feet AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. The CFI ACS asks for an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet AGL (AI.X.F.S2). Teach and fly the ACS number. Application: the AFH says the first turn of a spin loses about 1,000 feet [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], so add that above the 3,000 foot floor in case the roll-off becomes a spin.

Medium bank means roughly 20 to 45 degrees [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. Application: about 30 degrees suits the demonstration, because it is the bank the AFH says a pilot should be reluctant to exceed at base-to-final altitude [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], so the learner sees the stall come from a 'normal-looking' turn.

callout.text: ACS S5, exactly: "Roll into a medium-banked turn, apply excess rudder in the turn while holding bank constant with opposite aileron input, and add elevator pressure to keep the nose from lowering." Note what holds the bank: the aileron, not the rudder.

Application: apply the rudder smoothly and progressively, as the AFH says [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A sudden boot of rudder makes the airplane snap before you can narrate the setup, and the learner sees only a violent wing drop.

check.q: Why does the AFH say not to extend the flaps for this demonstration?
check.a: To avoid the possibility of exceeding the airplane's limitations [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Recovery procedure (K5). At the stall: nose-down elevator to reduce the AOA until the stall warning is gone, remove the excessive rudder and level the wings, add power as needed, and return to the desired flightpath [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. That is the general stall template, adapted [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]:

bullets: AOA first: reducing AOA is crucial for every stall recovery [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. With crossed controls this is what stops the roll from finishing.
Rudder out, wings level: cancel yaw with rudder to keep the stall from becoming a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Here that means taking out the excess rudder you put in.
Ailerons after the AOA: using aileron before the AOA is reduced can make the stall worse; a down aileron on the dropping wing raises its AOA and can roll it further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Power as needed: it reduces altitude loss but does not end the stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Flightpath: smooth, coordinated inputs, avoiding a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: Impending or full (S7). The evaluator chooses: recover at the first indication, or after a full stall has occurred (AI.X.F.S7), and you review this Area in the preflight briefing (CFI ACS Appendix 3, Area X note).
Risk in the stall recovery procedure (R1). The main risks are doing the steps out of order, pulling too hard afterwards, or letting it go too far:

bullets: Out of order: leveling the wings or adding power before reducing AOA are listed errors [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
Pull-out: abrupt pull-ups after a stall can cause secondary stalls and high loads [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; never let the airspeed or tachometer reach their red lines [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Too much push: excessive forward elevator gives low or negative G [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Spin: if rotation starts, follow the POH; the generic template is power idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, rudder neutral when rotation stops, then a smooth pull [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Start incipient spin recovery before 360 degrees of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

callout.text: In airplanes placarded against spins there is no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Your recovery must start at the first sign of the roll-off, not after it.

check.q: At the break the left wing drops and your learner instinctively adds right aileron with the nose still high. What is wrong with that?
check.a: Aileron before AOA reduction can deepen the stall: the down aileron on the left wing raises its AOA and can roll it further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Reduce AOA first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: Effect of environmental elements (R2). Each one makes the base-to-final trap more likely, or the demonstration less safe:

bullets: Turbulence: a vertical gust or wind shear can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall often comes while the pilot fights to hold the flightpath on a gusty approach; carry a higher approach speed in moderate to severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].
Microbursts: a pilot who reduced power and lowered the nose for the headwind shear is nose-low and power-low when the tailwind shear hits, which can cause a stall [[28:265|AWH 22-10]].

High density altitude: indicated stall speed does not change, but the true airspeed is higher for the same indicated airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. A higher speed at a given bank means a larger turn radius [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]. Application: on a hot, high day the base-to-final turn is wider at the same bank, so overshoots are more likely. Spin altitude losses are greater at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]], and the type of spin can change with density altitude [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

body.p: Aircraft limitations (R4). Check these before you fly the demonstration:

head: Limitation
Why it matters here
rows: Flaps
Not used, to avoid exceeding the airplane's limitations [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Maneuvering speed and large sideslips
Large, alternating inputs with large sideslip angles may cause structural failure at any speed, even below VA [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100f]]
Spin approval
Find it in the type certificate data sheet, the AFM/POH limitations or a placard [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Weight and CG

Aft CG makes stall entry easier and can lead to a flat spin, often unrecoverable [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]; an airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in the normal category may not recover from a spin that goes past one turn or 3 seconds, whichever is longer [[13:12|AC 61-67C 108]]
Red lines
Airspeed and tachometer never at their red lines during practice stalls [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]
Pull-out loads
A proper spin recovery typically loads about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]; avoid exceeding G and airspeed limits in the pull-out [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]

callout.text: Application: on the ramp, have the learner read the POH limitations page and the placards aloud, and tell you if this airplane is approved for spins. If it is not, say so in the brief: that is the reason we recover at the first hint of roll-off.

check.q: Where does the AFH say to look to find out if an airplane is approved for spins?
check.a: The type certificate data sheet or aircraft specifications, the limitations section of the AFM/POH, or a placard in clear view of the pilot [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

body.p: Collision hazards (R3) and clearing (S1). The demonstration descends and can end in a sudden roll, so clear at and below your altitude [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] and clear while slowing [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Clearing should come before all turns and before stalls and spins [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Raise the wing toward the turn in a high-wing airplane, lower it in a low-wing airplane, and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Many programs use two 90 degree turns in opposite directions; the instructor should insist on a clearing procedure [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. Haze makes practice areas worse [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], and you and the learner share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].
Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness, or disorientation (R5):

bullets: Distractions: most stall/spin accidents happened when the pilot's attention was diverted; 60 percent happened during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. The base-to-final turn is exactly where a radio call, traffic or a checklist pulls the eyes inside.
Task prioritization: once airborne, budgeting time and prioritizing tasks may allow enough time to finish them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Teach: fly the turn first, talk second.
Loss of situational awareness: knowing position, flightpath and other aircraft [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Losing it and not returning to the desired flightpath is a listed stall error [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

Disorientation: a head movement in a prolonged turn, such as looking down to pick something up, can trigger the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. In a spin, use the turn indicator, not the ball, to find the direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

callout.text: Do not teach this at the wrong time or altitude. The AIH warns against teaching stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room to recover [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

check.q: Why is a dropped item in the base-to-final turn a double hazard?
check.a: It diverts attention, the cause of most stall/spin accidents [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], and the head movement in a turn can cause the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

chunks.title: Fly it while you explain it

body.p: Demonstrate exactly the way you briefed it, in the same order, explaining power settings and attitudes as you go [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. A sample script, built on the AFH procedure [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]:

bullets: 1. Brief in the air: 'Same setup as on the ground. You follow me lightly on the controls. I will take it to the stall and recover.' (S8)
2. 'Clearing left and right, nothing below. Ground here is 1,200 MSL, so we finish no lower than 4,200.' (S1, S2)
3. 'Throttle back, gear down, throttle closed, flaps stay up. Holding altitude to glide speed... trimmed.' (S3, S4)
4. 'Here is our base to final. Medium bank, about 30 degrees, and we have overshot the centerline.' (S5)

5. 'Watch my feet: more and more left rudder. The bank wants to steepen, so I hold it with right aileron. Nose wants to drop, so I pull. Ball is out to the right. Feel the push to the outside.' (S5, S6)
6. 'Horn... buffet... and there it goes.' (S6)
7. 'Nose down until the horn stops, rudder out, wings level, power, climb back.' Or, if asked for an impending stall, recover at the first cue (S7).
8. 'In the pattern, that roll would have been into the ground. The cure was a go-around before any of this.' (S8)

head: Element
CFI ACS standard (AI.X.F)
rows: S2 Entry altitude
Task completed no lower than 3,000 feet AGL
S3 Configuration
Gear down, throttle closed
S4 Speed
Normal glide airspeed, trimmed
S5 Setup
Medium-banked turn, excess rudder in the turn, bank held constant with opposite aileron, elevator to keep the nose up
S6 Cues
Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall
S7 Recovery
At the first indication or after a full stall, as specified by the evaluator

callout.text: Application: if the demonstration does not go as briefed, for example the airplane stalls before you called the cue, say so right away and explain what happened. The AIH asks you to acknowledge and explain any deviation from your explanation [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

check.q: In the ACS setup, which control holds the bank constant once the excess rudder is in?
check.a: Opposite aileron input; elevator keeps the nose from lowering (AI.X.F.S5) [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Ground first. Learning stalls in the airplane only is slower than discussing their types and aerodynamics on the ground first, and you should review the task before the flight even if it was taught in ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For this stall the ground lesson carries most of the value, because the learner may see it in the air only once or twice.
A building-block flight sequence, following AC 61-67C's plan for gliding turn stalls [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200d]]:

head: Block
What the learner sees
Teaching point
rows: 1. Coordinated gliding turn stall
Both wings stall nearly together; the nose pitches down [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
The baseline: ball centered
2. Slipping gliding turn stall
The outer wing may stall first and drop [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]
Ball to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]
3. Skidding cross-control stall
The bank increases, the low wing drops, roll toward inverted [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Ball to the outside; this is the base-to-final killer
4. Back on the ground
Draw the pattern with a tailwind on base
Name the go-around trigger: any overshoot that would need more than 30 degrees or any rudder to fix [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]

body.p: Use the learner-tells, instructor-does step for this Task: let the learner talk you through the setup while you fly. It lets you check their understanding and correct a misunderstanding before they are absorbed in controlling the airplane [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. Whether the learner then flies the stall is your judgment and your syllabus; the AFH calls it a demonstration-only maneuver [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Check understanding, not memory. A learner may fly a maneuver correctly without understanding it; have them vary it or apply it elsewhere [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Application: after the demonstration, ask them to fly a normal gliding turn and deliberately show you a small skid at altitude, then fix it with rudder. That is the skill that prevents the stall.

Common errors related to this Task (K6) are in the last section. Brief the two most important before flight: too much rudder in glides [[24:85|AFH 3-24]], and leveling the wings before reducing AOA [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

callout.text: Application: when you debrief, ask the learner which three inputs created the stall (inside rudder, opposite aileron, back elevator) and which one decision would have prevented all three (the go-around).

check.q: AC 61-67C asks for gliding turn stalls in three ways. Which three, and what must you explain for each?
check.a: Coordinated, slipping and skidding; explain the ball position and the airplane's behavior in each stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200d]].

body.p: This demonstration is sudden: a roll toward inverted with little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. An anxious learner reacting to stalls may go into a fight-or-flight response [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Before stalls, review the aerodynamics, then describe the physical sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. For this one, tell them plainly: 'the wing will drop fast and the nose will go down. That is what we want you to see. I will have it back level in a couple of seconds.'

bullets: Brief the exchange of controls before the flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. During the demonstration, the learner follows lightly; you are flying.
Guard the controls and be ready to take over; anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and there is nothing to gain by fighting them for control [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Watch the feet. A learner who stiffens may jam a rudder pedal, the one input that feeds this stall. Application: brief 'feet light on the pedals' and say it again before the entry.
Be especially ready to take control on a learner's first attempt at a hazardous maneuver [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Never exceed your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Familiarize yourself with the airplane model before instructing in it, from the POH up to flight time in it [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Application: if you have not flown this stall in this make and model, fly it with another instructor first.

callout.text: The ACS reminds both the instructor and the evaluator to always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and loss of control (CFI ACS Appendix 2). A demonstration that goes past the first turn of rotation is no longer a demonstration.

check.q: Your learner tenses at the wing drop and pushes the pedal on the low-wing side. What do you do?
check.a: Take the controls and calmly say 'I have the flight controls' [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], then reduce AOA, take out the rudder and level the wings [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: On the checkride the evaluator may play your learner and make these errors; you analyze and correct them (S9). Built from the AFH stall error list [[24:126|AFH 5-21]], the gliding turn errors [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] and the cross-control text [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]:

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Failure to adequately clear the area
Straight into the glide with no clearing turns
Clear at and below before every stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Entry too low
Altimeter shows less than 3,000 ft AGL plus a spin margin
Climb first; a spin's first turn loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]
Flaps extended for realism
Flap lever moved during the setup
Flaps stay up, to stay inside the limitations [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Abrupt rudder
A sudden pedal stab and an early, violent wing drop
Apply the excess rudder smoothly and build the pressures together [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Letting the bank change
Bank steepens with the rudder instead of staying constant
Hold the bank with opposite aileron (AI.X.F.S5) [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Leveling the wings before reducing AOA
Aileron moves first, nose still high, the low wing drops further
Nose down until the warning stops, then wings [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]
Leaving the rudder in
Ball still out after the break, yaw continues
Remove the excessive rudder as you level the wings [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Power before AOA
Throttle forward first
AOA first; power does not end a stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Excessive forward pressure
Low or negative G, things float
Push only until the stall warning is gone [[24:121|AFH 5-16]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Secondary stall or hard pull-out
Second buffet as the nose comes up
Let flying speed return before raising the nose [[24:126|AFH 5-21]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]
Excessive airspeed buildup
Long dive after the roll-off
Dive only to cruise or maneuvering speed, with a gradual pull-up once the airspeed is safely above stalling [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]
Excess rudder in gliding turns (the root cause)
Ball outside during ordinary glides
Teach lighter rudder forces without power [[24:84|AFH 3-23]] [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]
Cross-controlling in gliding turns near the ground
Rudder in, opposite aileron, on base to final
Go around; bank 30 degrees or less, never skid [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]

body.p: Look for the root cause, not the symptom. The AIH says it is easy to tell whether an error is a misconception or a lack of motor skill when the learner says what they are doing out loud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. A learner who says 'more rudder to line up' has a misconception; a learner who says 'coordinated' while the ball is out has a feel problem.

callout.text: Application: safety permitting, let a learner go a little way into a skid in a gliding turn at altitude and find the fix; it is hard to learn a maneuver properly without the chance to correct an error [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. Never do this near a full stall or in the pattern.

check.q: During recovery, the learner's ball stays well out of center and the nose keeps yawing. Which step did they skip?
check.a: Removing the excessive rudder while leveling the wings [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], which cancels the yaw that leads to a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-35. Normal, slipping, and skidding turns at a constant altitude. (PHAK 5-24)
f1.alt: Three panels of a banked airplane seen from behind with force arrows. Normal turn: centrifugal force equals horizontal lift. Slipping turn: centrifugal force less than horizontal lift. Skidding turn: centrifugal force greater than horizontal lift. Each shows lift, vertical lift, horizontal lift, weight and load.

f2.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f2.alt: Three columns: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude display, a turn coordinator and a seat. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn, pilot feels a sideways force to the outside. Coordinated: ball centered, force straight down into the seat. Slip: ball to the inside, force to the inside.

f3.caption: Figure 3-15. Overbanking tendency. (AFH 3-14)
f3.alt: A banked high-wing airplane with a curved arrow showing the roll. A box at the top says the outer wing travels a greater distance, with higher speed and more lift. A box at the bottom says the inner wing travels a shorter distance, with lower speed and less lift.

f4.caption: Figure 5-15. Spin, an aggravated stall and autorotation. (AFH 5-22)
f4.alt: An airplane descending nose low around a vertical pole, with a yellow ribbon spiraling around the pole to show its corkscrew path.

f5.caption: Figure 5-10. Stall recovery template. (AFH 5-15)
f5.alt: A table titled Stall Recovery Template: 1 wing leveler or autopilot, disconnect; 2a pitch nose-down, apply until impending stall indications are eliminated; 2b trim nose-down pitch, as needed; 3 bank, wings level; 4 thrust or power, as needed; 5 speed brakes or spoilers, retract; 6 return to the desired flight path.

f6.caption: Figure 5-16. Spin entry and recovery. (AFH 5-23)
f6.alt: An airplane stalls and enters a spin around a vertical column. Boxes describe the incipient spin (about 4 to 6 seconds and about 2 turns in light aircraft), the fully developed spin (airspeed, vertical speed and rotation stabilized; small training aircraft lose about 500 feet per 3-second turn) and recovery (training aircraft usually recover in about a quarter to half a turn after anti-spin inputs). An inset shows the descending wing more stalled at a greater angle of attack and the rising wing less stalled.

f7.caption: Figure 9-8. Positive exchange of flight controls. (AIH 9-9)
f7.alt: Three stacked panels: the instructor says 'You have the flight controls', the learner says 'I have the flight controls', and the instructor again says 'You have the flight controls'.

scenario.title: A tailwind on base, then a demonstration on a hot afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. On this morning's pattern flight your pre-solo learner overshot final twice in a strong wind that was a tailwind on base, and the second time you felt them push the inside rudder hard while holding opposite aileron. You plan a cross-control stall demonstration for this afternoon in a fixed-gear, high-wing trainer placarded against intentional spins. It will be hot, the practice area terrain tops out at 1,400 ft MSL, there are scattered clouds at 5,000 ft MSL, and there is light chop below 4,000 ft MSL.

questions.q: What exactly went wrong in the morning pattern, in the AFH's terms?
questions.a: An unrecognized tailwind gave a higher groundspeed on base, so the turn came late; the learner tried to fix the overshoot with inside rudder and opposite aileron, the skidding setup that leads to a cross-control stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The fix was a go-around and not more than 30 degrees of bank [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: Using the ACS floor and a one-turn spin margin, where must you enter, and does the 5,000 ft MSL cloud base allow it?
questions.a: The ACS asks for completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.F.S2): 1,400 + 3,000 = 4,400 ft MSL. Adding about 1,000 ft for a first turn of spin [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] puts entry near 5,400 ft MSL, above the 5,000 ft cloud base. Do not teach stalls below a cloud layer that leaves too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; find a higher gap, another area or change the lesson [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: How does the hot afternoon change your planning?
questions.a: Indicated stall speed is the same, but true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]], so turns are wider at the same bank [[24:75|AFH 3-14]]; spin altitude losses are greater at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Plan a bigger altitude margin.

questions.q: The airplane is placarded against intentional spins. What does that mean for the demonstration?
questions.a: There is no assurance of recovery from a fully developed spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Recover at the first sign of roll-off, before rotation develops, and brief the POH spin recovery anyway [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

questions.q: The chop is below 4,000 ft MSL. Why does it matter for a stall demonstration and for the learner's patterns?
questions.a: A vertical gust can suddenly raise the AOA, and the stall may come while the pilot fights to hold the flightpath; use a higher approach speed in turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

questions.q: On the way back, the learner drops their pen on base and bends down to get it. What risks does that create, and what do you teach?
questions.a: Diverted attention is behind most stall/spin accidents, which mostly happen in takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], and a head movement in a turn can cause the coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Fly first; budget and prioritize tasks [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

skills.do: Clear the area at and below your altitude before slowing, and say what you are looking for.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns with spoken callouts every time, the way you want a learner to copy them [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed "no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)", and explain how you added a spin margin.
skills.practice: Before each flight, write down the practice area's highest terrain and work out the entry altitude with a spin margin [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

skills.do: "Configure the airplane (with gear down) and close the throttle", keeping the flaps up and saying why.
skills.practice: Run the setup flow aloud on the ground with the POH limitations page open [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

skills.do: "Establish a normal glide airspeed and trim the airplane" while holding altitude until the speed decays.
skills.practice: Practice glides from level flight to a trimmed, stable glide speed with the ball centered [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

skills.do: "Roll into a medium-banked turn, apply excess rudder in the turn while holding bank constant with opposite aileron input, and add elevator pressure to keep the nose from lowering", narrating each input.
skills.practice: With another instructor, fly the entry several times, recovering at the first cue, until the inputs are smooth and the bank stays constant [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

skills.do: "Acknowledge the cues at the first indication of a stall (e.g., aircraft buffet, stall horn, etc.)" by calling each one out loud.
skills.practice: Call the ball position, horn and buffet aloud on every stall you fly, including coordinated ones [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

skills.do: "Recover at the first indication of a stall or after a full stall has occurred, as specified by the evaluator": AOA first, excess rudder out, wings level, power, flightpath.
skills.practice: Practice both versions, and say the evaluator's request back before every entry [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

skills.do: "Describe and demonstrate conditions that lead to a cross-controlled stall for future avoidance": the tailwind base, the overshoot, the skid, and the go-around that prevents it.
skills.practice: Teach the base-to-final story to a friend on a whiteboard in under three minutes [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]].

skills.do: "Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task" when the evaluator plays a learner who levels the wings first, leaves the rudder in or enters too low.
skills.practice: Have a fellow applicant fly the maneuver with planted errors while you call and fix them [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

quiz.q: In the AFH's base-to-final story, what usually starts the overshoot that tempts the pilot to skid?
options: A headwind on base that slows the groundspeed so much that the pilot turns final far too early
Extending full flaps on base, which balloons the airplane up and carries it past the centerline
An unrecognized tailwind on base, giving a higher groundspeed and a late or shallow turn
A strong crosswind on final that drifts the airplane well off the extended runway centerline
quiz.why: There may be an unrecognized tailwind component and higher groundspeed on base, so the pilot turns late or with inadequate bank and overshoots [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: In PHAK Figure 5-35, what defines the skidding turn?
options: Centrifugal force is greater than the horizontal component of lift
The horizontal component of lift is greater than the centrifugal force acting on it
Vertical lift is greater than the weight of the airplane
The load factor is less than 1 G during the turn
quiz.why: A skidding turn results from an excess of centrifugal force over the horizontal lift component [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].

quiz.q: In the base-to-final scenario, what does the pilot's back elevator pressure do once the nose slices down?
options: It lowers the AOA and gives back aileron effectiveness on both wings
It removes the skid by pulling the nose toward the turn
It holds the bank angle constant against overbanking
It increases the AOA toward critical, setting up the stall
quiz.why: The natural reaction to the nose dropping is to pull back, increasing the AOA toward critical [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: The PHAK describes what happens when rudder yaws an airplane to one side. Which wing gains airspeed?
options: The wing that swings back, because it is shielded behind the fuselage from the relative wind
The wing that swings forward, which then presents a longer leading edge to the airflow
Neither wing, because yaw only changes the heading and not the airspeed over either wing
Both wings equally, because the propeller slipstream speeds up the whole wing during the yaw
quiz.why: When turbulence or rudder application yaws the aircraft, the opposite wing presents a longer leading edge to the airflow and the airspeed of the forward wing increases [[1:117|PHAK 5-20]]. In a skidding turn that is the outside wing.

quiz.q: Which situation is listed in the AFH as a common error in power-off accuracy approaches?
options: Using a 30 degree bank on the base-to-final turn with a strong headwind
Using full flaps on final with a gusty wind
Skidding turns in an effort to increase gliding distance
Turning base at a point 45 degrees from the runway
quiz.why: 'Skidding turns in an effort to increase gliding distance' is a listed error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: What range of bank does the AFH call a medium turn?
options: Less than about 20 degrees
About 20 to 45 degrees
About 30 to 60 degrees
About 45 degrees or more
quiz.why: Medium turns result from a bank between approximately 20 and 45 degrees [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

quiz.q: In a power-off landing approach, what does the AFH say excessive rudder pedal pressure does to the bank?
options: It lowers the lift on both wings equally, so the bank stays where the pilot put it
It yaws the nose but leaves the bank unchanged unless the pilot moves the ailerons
It rolls the airplane away from the rudder, so the pilot needs aileron toward the turn
It increases lift on the outside wing and banks the airplane toward the rudder
quiz.why: Excessive rudder pressure leads to increased lift on the outside wing, banking the airplane in the direction of the rudder deflection; the pilot may then hold opposite aileron and add back pressure [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

quiz.q: In the AFH entry procedure, what is the medium-banked turn meant to simulate?
options: A final approach turn that overshoots the runway centerline
A turn back to the runway after an engine failure on takeoff
A steep turn in cruise used to clear the area before the stall
A climbing turn to pattern altitude during a go-around
quiz.why: Once the glide is stabilized, the airplane is rolled into a medium-banked turn to simulate a final approach turn that overshoots the centerline of the runway [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: AC 61-67C describes stall/spin accidents in the turn from base to final. Why did those pilots rudder the airplane around in a skid?
options: To keep the airspeed up, because a skid has less drag than a normal coordinated turn
To lose altitude faster, because they were high on the approach to the runway
So as not to overshoot the runway nor use an excessive bank angle in the pattern
Because the ailerons had stopped working at the slow approach speed they flew
quiz.why: Stall/spin accidents have occurred during a turn from base to final because the pilot tried to rudder the airplane around (skid) so as not to overshoot the runway nor use excessive bank angle in the traffic pattern [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

quiz.q: Which practiced stall does the AFH say builds awareness of what can happen when the controls are misused in the turn from base to final?
options: Power-off turning stalls
Power-on straight-ahead stalls
Power-off straight-ahead stalls
Power-on climbing turn stalls
quiz.why: Power-off turning stalls develop the pilot's awareness of what could happen if the controls are improperly used during a turn from the base leg to the final approach [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner reads AC 61-67C paragraph 109 and the AFH cross-control section and says they describe the skid's controls differently. What is the difference?
options: The AC says the aileron is neutral in a skid, while the AFH says it is full against the turn
The AC says aileron and rudder go the same direction in a skid; the AFH has them opposite
The AC calls a skid a slip, while the AFH uses skid only for a turn with too much bank
There is none: both say opposite aileron is held against the rudder in every skidding turn
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C: 'In a skidding turn, where both aileron and rudder are applied in the same direction' [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. AFH: a cross-control stall has aileron pressure one way and rudder the other [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Both say the spin usually goes the way of the rudder.

final_quiz.q: Your learner's AFH says to practice stalls so recovery is no lower than 1,500 ft AGL. What floor do you use for this demonstration on your CFI checkride?
options: 1,500 ft AGL, because the AFH number governs every stall flown in a single-engine airplane
2,000 ft AGL, the AFH 1,500 ft plus 500 ft for one turn of a spin as AC 61-67C estimates
1,500 ft AGL plus whatever altitude loss the POH lists for a power-off stall recovery
Completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL, as the CFI ACS states for this Task
final_quiz.why: The AFH recommends 1,500 ft AGL for stall practice [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], but the CFI ACS for this Task asks for completion no lower than 3,000 ft AGL (AI.X.F.S2). Teach and fly the ACS number.

final_quiz.q: Your demonstration goes too far: the low wing keeps dropping and the airplane starts to rotate. In the AFH's spin section, when should incipient spin recovery begin?
options: Before completing 360 degrees of rotation
After two full turns, once the spin is stable
Only once the airspeed starts to increase
After the ball shows which way it is turning
final_quiz.why: The pilot should initiate incipient spin recovery procedures prior to completing 360 degrees of rotation, applying full rudder opposite the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. The ball is not used to find the direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

final_quiz.q: On a practice power-off approach, your learner holds left rudder and right aileron in the gliding turn to final at 400 ft AGL. Which listed AFH descent error is this?
options: Failure to slow the airplane to approximate glide speed before lowering pitch
Attempting to stretch the glide by applying more back-elevator pressure
Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground
Inability to sense changes in airspeed through sound and feel
final_quiz.why: 'Cross-controlling during gliding turns near the ground' is on the AFH list of common errors in descents and descending turns [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says stall/spin accidents are rare now that trainers are spin resistant. Which PHAK figure do you give them?
options: Stall/spin accidents are now under 5 percent of general aviation fatal accidents
Over 25 percent of GA fatal accidents happen in maneuvering, and half of those are stall/spin
About 60 percent of GA fatal accidents are stall/spin during practice stalls at altitude
Stall/spin accidents happen mainly in cruise, so the pattern is the safest place
final_quiz.why: More than 25 percent of general aviation fatal accidents occur during the maneuvering phase of flight, and half of those involve stall/spin scenarios [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks why you are showing a stall they will never fly on their own checkride. Which answer states the AFH objective?
options: To build the skill to recover from a fully developed spin in any light airplane
To practice the recovery to a set heading, as on a commercial practical test
To find the airplane's exact stall speed in a skid for the pattern
To show what uncoordinated flight does to stall behavior and why turns must stay coordinated
final_quiz.why: The objective is to show the effects of uncoordinated flight on stall behavior and to emphasize the importance of maintaining coordinated flight while making turns [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: Which of these is described by the AFH as a gliding-turn hazard that can rapidly turn into an unrecoverable spin?
options: A shallow, coordinated gliding turn at best glide speed after an engine failure
A low-level gliding steep turn with rudder toward the bank while pulling to hold altitude
A straight glide at best glide speed with a 10 percent level-off lead
A coordinated climbing turn to pattern altitude with full power
final_quiz.why: A low-level gliding steep turn with excessive rudder toward the bank and back pressure to hold altitude can rapidly become an unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

final_quiz.q: During your demonstration your learner follows along on the controls. What does the AIH say about the learner manipulating the controls during maneuvers?
options: It may be a significant hazard, so keep track of it
It is no hazard during an instructor demonstration
It matters only during takeoffs and landings
It is a hazard only for learners who have soloed
final_quiz.why: Among the concepts for teaching most maneuvers, the AIH says to keep track of hazards during maneuvering, and that the learner manipulating controls may be a significant hazard [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

final_quiz.q: Which CFI ACS Appendix 2 rule applies to both you and the evaluator throughout this demonstration?
options: Spins may be entered only when the evaluator calls them, and never at the applicant's request
Every stall must be taken to a full stall so the evaluator can judge the recovery
Always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and loss of control
Any stall warning during the setup turn is automatically unsatisfactory for the applicant
final_quiz.why: Appendix 2 says the applicant and the instructor or evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin and inadvertent loss of control (CFI ACS Appendix 2). The AFH agrees: proficiency in avoiding conditions that could lead to an accidental stall/spin is essential [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Where does the AFH say that held, uncoordinated control deflections, with their potential for a spin, are especially hazardous?
options: In cruise at high altitude, where the air is thinner
During engine run-up, with the brakes held on the ramp
In steep turns at maneuvering speed in a practice area
At low altitude, such as in the traffic pattern
final_quiz.why: Pilots who maintain certain uncoordinated control deflections create the potential for a spin, which is especially hazardous at low altitudes, such as in the traffic pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

final_quiz.q: In AC 61-67C's training plan for stalls in gliding turns, what do you demonstrate besides the skidding turn stall?
options: A power-on departure stall followed by an accelerated stall in a steep turn
Stalls from coordinated and slipping turns, with the ball position in each
An elevator trim stall and a secondary stall, each with flaps fully extended
A fully developed spin in each direction, from a coordinated gliding turn
final_quiz.why: Perform the stalls from a coordinated, a slipping and a skidding turn, and explain the ball position and airplane behavior in each [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200d]].

final_quiz.q: Building your ground lesson, you want an AC 61-67C example of a distraction that sets up an inadvertent stall near this Task's real-world setting. Which is on its list?
options: Flying a traffic pattern on a windy day
Taxiing out with a strong quartering tailwind
Flying straight and level in cruise on autopilot
Climbing at VY in smooth air with the checklist done
final_quiz.why: AC 61-67C lists distractions such as locating a checklist, flying a traffic pattern on a windy day, reading a chart, and retrieving items from the floor, back seat or glove compartment [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator asks you to configure per S3 in a fixed-gear trainer with flaps. What do you do?
options: Extend full flaps and leave the throttle at cruise power
Set half flaps and climb power so the stall comes slowly
Close the throttle and leave the flaps up; the gear is already down
Retrim nose-down and add power to hold altitude in the turn
final_quiz.why: S3 says configure the airplane (with gear down) and close the throttle (AI.X.F.S3); the AFH says not to extend the flaps, to avoid exceeding the airplane's limitations [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: The cross-control stall shows why turns must stay coordinated; only CFI applicants may be tested on it.
The real setup is a tailwind base, a late turn, then inside rudder, opposite aileron and back pressure.
Inside rudder gives the outside wing more lift, so the bank steepens on its own, and at the stall the airplane can roll toward inverted.
A stall in a skid can spin the way the rudder points, regardless of which wingtip is up.
Demonstrate it power off, flaps up, finishing no lower than 3,000 ft AGL with a spin margin.
Recover with AOA first, then excess rudder out and wings level, then power.
The cure in the pattern is a go-around, not more bank or more rudder.
cfi_notes: Altitude: the AFH says "It is recommended that stalls be practiced at an altitude that allows recovery no lower than 1,500 feet AGL for single-engine airplanes, or higher if recommended by the AFM/POH" [[24:121|AFH 5-16]], and that "all spins should begin at an altitude high enough to complete recovery at or above 1,500 feet AGL" [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. AC 61-67C paragraph 103 uses the same 1,500 feet AGL for intentional full stalls in single-engine airplanes [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]]. The CFI ACS for this Task says: "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 3,000 feet above ground level (AGL)" (AI.X.F.S2). For the checkride, teach and fly the ACS 3,000 feet, plus a spin margin.

AC 61-67C paragraph 109 says: "In a skidding turn, where both aileron and rudder are applied in the same direction, rotation will be in the direction the controls are applied. However, in a slipping turn, where opposite aileron is held against the rudder, the resultant spin will usually occur in the direction opposite the aileron that is being applied" [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. The AFH describes the skidding cross-control stall with "aileron pressure applied in one direction and rudder pressure in the opposite direction" [[24:125|AFH 5-20]], and the ACS S5 says "holding bank constant with opposite aileron input". Both sources agree the spin from cross controlling usually goes the way of the rudder [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]] [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Teach the AFH and ACS description of the controls.

Spin altitude loss, three numbers from three places: the AFH text says "the first turn in a spin results in an altitude loss of approximately 1,000 feet, while each subsequent turn loses about half that amount" and names no airplane type [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; AFH Figure 5-16 on the same page says small training aircraft in a fully developed spin lose approximately 500 feet per 3-second turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; AC 61-67C gives "approximately 500 feet per each 3-second turn" as a rough estimate for most small aircraft in which spins are authorized, with greater losses at higher density altitudes [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Plan this demonstration with the larger AFH first-turn figure.

Recovery order: AC 61-67C paragraph 105 puts maximum allowable power right after reducing AOA [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]]; the AFH cross-control procedure and template level the wings and remove rudder before adding power as needed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Teach the AFH order.
The ACS S3 names only gear down and throttle closed; flaps are not mentioned. The AFH says do not extend them [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Brief 'flaps up' with the evaluator.

No source states in words which wing stalls first in a skidding cross-control stall. The sources do state that inside rudder gives the outside wing more lift and banks the airplane toward the rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]] [[1:117|PHAK 5-20]], and that the airplane may roll toward inverted at the stall [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. The slower inside wing [[24:75|AFH 3-14]] plus its down aileron raising its AOA [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] is a reasoned explanation for the low wing going first; present it to learners as reasoning, not as an FAA statement.

Unlike Tasks such as AI.X.E, the ACS skills line for this Task reads 'The applicant exhibits the skill to', not 'demonstrates and simultaneously explains'. Narrate anyway: S8 asks you to describe the conditions, and your learners copy what you show [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

The AFH notes rudder forces are lighter in glides, so learners apply too much rudder [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Many cross-control habits start in ordinary gliding turns, long before the stall lesson. Watch the ball on every power-off approach.
gaps: None of these sources gives the altitude lost in a cross-control stall recovery in a light trainer. Measure your airplane's at altitude with another instructor.
How a particular airplane behaves in a skidding stall, and whether it is approved for spins, comes from the POH/AFM and placards, not from the handbooks.
The sources give no number for 'excess rudder' and no single bank angle; 'medium-banked' is the only guide. Agree the setup with the evaluator.
The sources do not say whether a learner should fly this stall themselves or how many times to show it; the AFH only calls it demonstration-only. Follow your syllabus.
No source gives a script for narrating the demonstration or the exact words to brief before it. Write your own and use it every time.

activities.title: True or false: the setup and the forces
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The AFH says held, uncoordinated control deflections create spin potential that is especially hazardous at low altitude, such as in the traffic pattern.
In a correctly executed turn, the rudder supplies the force that turns the airplane.
cards.why: False. The horizontal component of lift turns the aircraft; the rudder only corrects the track of the nose and tail into the relative wind [[1:119|PHAK 5-22]].

cards.s: In the AFH demonstration, the rudder, opposite aileron and back elevator pressures are all increased until the airplane stalls.
cards.why: True. All of these control pressures should be increased until the airplane stalls [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

cards.s: AC 61-67C lists crossed-control turns from base leg to final among power-off stall/spin accident situations.
A skidding turn is corrected by more rate of turn and less bank.
cards.why: False. A skid is corrected by less rate of turn, more bank, or both [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]].

cards.s: Because the power is off, a cross-control stall on a gliding approach cannot turn into a spin.
cards.why: False. In the power-off approach cross-control condition, a stall almost certainly results in a rapid and unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

steps: Choose an altitude to finish no lower than 3,000 ft AGL with a spin margin
Clear the area while slowly retarding the throttle

At the stall: nose down until the warning stops, rudder out, wings level, power

activities.title: Numbers for the brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: PHAK stall table: gear and flaps up, power off, wings level, the stall speed is 65 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor, and the level-turn load factor is 1 divided by the cosine of the bank. Predict the stall speed in a 30 degree bank.
items.why: 1 / cos 30 = 1.155; square root = 1.075; 65 x 1.075 = 69.8, about 70 knots, which matches the table [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]] [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

items.q: Same airplane and method, 45 degrees of bank, the bank a learner might roll into trying to fix an overshoot. What is the predicted stall speed?
items.why: 1 / cos 45 = 1.414; square root = 1.189; 65 x 1.189 = 77.3, about 77 knots, matching the table [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

items.q: Practice area terrain tops out at 1,350 ft MSL. What is the lowest MSL altitude at which the ACS lets you complete the Task?
Same area. You want room for one turn of spin before reaching that floor. Using the AFH's figure for the first turn, what is your minimum entry altitude?
items.why: First spin turn loses about 1,000 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]: 4,350 + 1,000 = 5,350 ft MSL.

items.q: Same airplane (65 knots wings level, gear and flaps up, power off). The overbanking runs away and the bank reaches 50 degrees. Using the same method for a level turn, what is the predicted stall speed?
items.why: 1 / cos 50 = 1.556; square root = 1.247; 65 x 1.247 = 81.1, about 81 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. The PHAK table has no 50 degree column; this is the formula only.

activities.title: CFI checkride: the evaluator plays your learner
activities.intro: You are the CFI applicant. The evaluator acts as a private pilot learner who has never seen a cross-control stall. Terrain in the practice area tops out at 1,500 ft MSL; the airplane is placarded against spins.

steps.s: Level at 6,200 ft MSL and clear of traffic, the 'learner' closes the throttle and pushes straight into a steep glide 20 knots fast. What do you say?
options: Fine, extra speed gives a bigger stall margin for the turn
Add some power back so the glide is not so steep
Hold altitude until the speed nears normal glide, then set the glide and retrim
Roll into the turn now and let the speed bleed off in it
steps.why: Close the throttle and maintain altitude until the airspeed approaches the normal glide speed, then retrim as the glide is set [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; S4 asks for a normal glide airspeed, trimmed (AI.X.F.S4).

steps.s: Gliding and trimmed, the 'learner' reaches for full flaps 'to make it like a real final'. Your reply?
options: Flaps stay up, to avoid exceeding the airplane's limitations
Use half flaps as a compromise between realism and safety
Good idea, a real final usually has full flaps out
Flaps are fine as long as the speed is in the white arc
steps.why: The AFH says not to extend the flaps, to avoid the possibility of exceeding the airplane's limitations [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: In the turn, the 'learner' adds rudder and lets the bank steepen to 50 degrees. What do you correct?
options: Nothing, a steep bank shows the danger better
Reduce the rudder and recover immediately
Add power to hold altitude in the steep bank
Hold the bank constant with opposite aileron, as the ACS describes
steps.why: The setup holds the bank constant with opposite aileron (AI.X.F.S5) [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

steps.s: At the break the left wing drops. The 'learner' lowers the nose until the horn stops but keeps the left rudder in; the ball is far right and the nose keeps yawing left. What do you say?
options: Hold it: the yaw will stop by itself once the speed builds
Remove the excess rudder as you level the wings, then power as needed
Add full power first, then deal with the rudder
Push the nose further down until the yaw stops
steps.why: After the AOA is reduced, remove the excessive rudder input, level the wings and add power as needed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]; cancel yaw with rudder so the stall does not progress into a spin [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

steps.s: In the debrief the 'learner' asks what would have kept them out of this on a real base-to-final turn. Your best answer?
options: Use more rudder and less bank when you overshoot
Fly faster in the pattern so you never stall
Plan the base for the wind, keep bank at 30 degrees or less, never skid, and go around after an overshoot
Slip instead of skid, since slips cannot stall
steps.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; avoid more than 30 degrees of bank and skidding turns [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
